The central question is: why do transformers trained on algorithmic tasks (sorting, addition, logical inference) with sequences of length ≤N systematically fail at length N+k, even when the underlying rule is identical and the model has ostensibly "learned" it? The suspected culprit is positional encoding — both absolute (APE) and relative (RPE) schemes inject position-dependent signal that the model exploits as a shortcut, binding computational roles to specific positions rather than learning position-invariant operations. An expert recognizes that this isn't simply "the model hasn't seen longer inputs" — it's that attention patterns, which must route information between tokens, are shaped by position-biased dot products, so the circuits that implement, say, carry propagation in binary addition are geometrically misconfigured when the sequence extends beyond the training distribution. The subtle thing a beginner misses is that generalization failure is often not uniform: models frequently succeed at N+1 or N+2 but collapse sharply at some threshold, which reveals that the failure is mechanistic and structured — tied to how positional geometry distorts specific algorithmic sub-circuits — rather than a smooth capacity limitation. Experts also worry about the confound between architectural failure (the encoding scheme itself) and training failure (insufficient curriculum diversity), because a model trained with random-length sampling can sometimes generalize further using the same architecture, implying the encoding's inductive bias is interacting with the optimization trajectory in ways that aren't yet formally characterized.

Mechanistic interpretability work on small transformers trained on multi-digit addition (e.g., Lee et al. 2023, "Teaching Arithmetic to Small Transformers") identifies a functional division where early-layer heads perform digit alignment — attending from each output position back to the corresponding operand digits — while mid-layer heads implement carry propagation by attending one position to the right, chaining dependency across digit columns. The carry heads are precisely the ones that break at length generalization: their attention patterns are calibrated to relative offsets seen during training, so a head trained to look "one position right within a 7-digit number" has its key-query dot products tuned to the specific positional encoding difference Δpos=1 at those absolute positions, not to the abstract relation "one column over." To distinguish a truly position-invariant carry head from a memorized one, you would intervene: copy a trained model's activations on an in-distribution 7-digit problem into a prefix of a 12-digit problem (activation patching), and check whether the carry signal propagates correctly in the novel positions — a memorized head will produce near-zero attention weight on the correct source token because the positional encoding at position 10 was never reinforced during training. Quantitatively, you can extract the attention score as a function of Δpos alone (marginalizing over content) and plot it: a position-invariant head yields a score that depends only on Δpos and not on the absolute positions of query and key, while a memorized head shows a peaked response only within the trained absolute-position range. Randomized position ablations (shuffling position embeddings at inference) also cleanly separate the two: invariant heads maintain carry accuracy because their keys and queries interact via content, while memorized heads collapse immediately because the content signal is weak and position was doing most of the discriminative work. The practical finding across these analyses is sobering — in standard APE transformers, virtually all carry heads fall into the memorized category, which is why even models that score 99%+ on trained lengths drop to near-chance on N+3 or N+4 without architectural intervention like NoPE or FIRE positional schemes.

The honest answer, supported by empirical work, is that RoPE and ALiBi shift the failure mode rather than eliminate it — the carry heads become memorized over relative offsets instead of absolute ones, which buys longer generalization but not invariance. Anil et al. (2022, "Exploring Length Generalization in Large Language Models") and subsequent ablations show that ALiBi-trained models on addition tasks generalize somewhat further than APE models, but still collapse at a threshold that scales roughly with training length, suggesting the model is exploiting the learned bias of the linear distance penalty rather than learning a content-driven carry rule. The mechanistic reason is that RoPE encodes position via rotation of the key and query vectors in frequency space, so a head's attention score between positions i and j depends on the inner product of their rotated embeddings at relative offset (i−j) — this is still a fixed function the model can overfit to, and during training on sequences of length ≤N, the model only ever reinforces weights at relative offsets ≤N−1, leaving the behavior at offset N undefined and typically wrong. ALiBi is arguably worse in this respect because its linear penalty is explicitly a function of distance, so a head that should attend at offset Δ=1 for carry propagation is discouraged from attending at Δ=1 when the absolute positions are large, because the penalty term grows with the raw index even though the relative offset is identical — this is a subtle but important asymmetry that breaks the "relative" promise in practice for tasks requiring uniform local attention across all positions. The clearest demonstration comes from Deletang et al. (2023, "Neural Networks and the Chomsky Hierarchy"), which benchmarks multiple encoding schemes on counter and stack tasks requiring strict length generalization: no standard positional encoding — absolute or relative — achieves clean out-of-distribution generalization, and the performance curves are qualitatively similar in shape, differing mainly in where the cliff occurs. Genuine position-invariance for carry heads appears to require either NoPE (no positional encoding, relying solely on causal masking and content) combined with scratchpad-style intermediate tokens, or explicit architectural constraints like universal transformers with tied weights, which force the same computation to execute at every position by construction rather than by learned coincidence.

Nothing in a NoPE model's architecture guarantees disambiguation of identical columns — and this is a real failure mode, not a theoretical one — but in practice the causal context to the left of each column breaks the symmetry, because the carry-in bit arriving from the previous column differs even when the current digits are identical. Concretely, in "3+7=...3+7=..." the second "3+7" column receives a carry-in of 1 (since 3+7=10 produces a carry), so the hidden state at that position encodes not just "3,7" but "3,7, carry=1," making it informationally distinct from the first column even with identical digit content; a carry head attending leftward reads this carry token and produces a different output. This is essentially the model exploiting contextual position — the accumulated computational history in the residual stream substitutes for explicit positional encoding, a mechanism explored in Haviv et al. (2022, "Transformer Language Models without Positional Encodings") who show NoPE models develop implicit position representations in their residual streams detectable by linear probing, even without injected positional signal. The failure case is at the start of computation where no left context exists yet, and for tasks with genuinely ambiguous prefixes — repeated substrings with no distinguishing carry history — NoPE models do show elevated error rates, which is why scratchpad formats (writing intermediate carry bits explicitly as tokens) are so effective: they convert implicit contextual state into explicit token content, giving the attention mechanism unambiguous keys to attend to. Feng et al. (2023, "Towards Revealing the Mystery of Chain-of-Thought") formalize this: scratchpad tokens in arithmetic tasks don't just help by reducing problem complexity, they inject positional information as content, which NoPE heads can attend to reliably across any length because the discriminating signal is now in the embedding, not the position encoding. The practical upshot is that NoPE + scratchpad is the most robust combination currently known for length generalization on addition, but it displaces rather than solves the core problem — you're now relying on the model to correctly generate the scratchpad carry tokens, and errors there cascade, so length generalization becomes bounded by scratchpad generation accuracy rather than positional encoding geometry.

Yes, scratchpad misformatting at length generalization is empirically documented and arguably the central failure mode of chain-of-thought on algorithmic tasks — Nye et al. (2021) note it in their original scratchpad paper, and Anil et al. (2022) show explicitly that models generating correct final answers sometimes produce scratchpads with internal carry errors that happen to cancel out, meaning the scratchpad is not faithfully implementing the algorithm even when the answer is right. The causal inertness question is exactly the right one to ask, and the cleanest test is scratchpad intervention: at inference time, generate the scratchpad up to step k, then surgically corrupt a single carry token (flip carry=1 to carry=0), and measure whether the final answer changes accordingly — a causally active scratchpad propagates the error forward and produces a wrong answer, while an inert one ignores the corruption and either recovers or was never using it. Lanham et al. (2023, "Measuring Faithfulness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning") run exactly this intervention class on reasoning tasks and find that models vary widely in scratchpad faithfulness, with some models showing near-zero sensitivity to mid-scratchpad corruptions, confirming that the scratchpad can be a post-hoc rationalization generated in parallel with rather than causally upstream of the answer. A subtler detection method is truncation testing: force the model to emit the final answer after only k of the expected T scratchpad steps and measure accuracy as a function of k — if accuracy rises sharply only after the carry-propagation steps are complete, the scratchpad is doing real causal work; if accuracy is already high at k=1 or k=2, the model is computing the answer via a parallel pathway and using the scratchpad for appearance. The misformatting failure at longer lengths has a specific signature: scratchpad token accuracy degrades roughly linearly with position (each step has some error probability p, so step t is correct with probability (1-p)^t), while final answer accuracy degrades faster than this linear model predicts, suggesting the errors compound rather than cancel — this superlinear degradation distinguishes genuine algorithmic scratchpad use from a model that ignores its own intermediate tokens.

If the scratchpad is causally inert, the implication is that the answer token's residual stream is being written to by attention heads that attend past the scratchpad directly to the input digits, with the scratchpad tokens contributing near-zero weight in those heads' attention patterns — mechanistically, the model has learned two parallel circuits, one that produces scratchpad tokens autoregressively and one that computes the answer from input, and these circuits share weights but not information flow. You can localize this by running path patching (as in Wang et al. 2022 on the IOI circuit) from the input digit positions to the answer token position while blocking information flow through scratchpad token positions: if answer accuracy is preserved under this scratchpad-bypass ablation, the direct input-to-answer circuit is sufficient and the scratchpad circuit is vestigial. The forcing question is harder and the most promising approach is architectural rather than loss-based: Pfau et al. (2023, "Let's Think Dot by Dot") experiment with opaque "filler tokens" that carry computation forward without being interpretable text, and find that when the model is forced to pass activations through a fixed-width bottleneck of intermediate tokens before seeing the answer position, it does route computation through them — but this works because the bottleneck is enforced by causal masking geometry, not by any training signal. A training-based forcing approach would require something like a scratchpad faithfulness loss — penalizing the model when its answer changes after scratchpad corruption, incentivizing sensitivity to intermediate tokens — but this is circular because computing the faithfulness penalty requires knowing the correct scratchpad content, which is exactly what you're trying to teach. The deepest implication is about residual stream depth: parallel bypass circuits tend to be shallow (1-2 layer attention shortcuts from input to output), while faithful scratchpad computation requires depth proportional to the number of algorithmic steps, so if you observe that ablating early-to-late direct attention paths kills answer accuracy, the computation was shallow and inert; if killing mid-layer paths through scratchpad positions kills it, the computation was genuinely sequential. This suggests a diagnostic: measure the minimum layer depth of the critical path from input to answer using activation patching across layers, and compare it to the theoretical minimum depth needed to implement the algorithm — a mismatch where the critical path is shallower than the algorithm requires is strong evidence for a bypass circuit exploiting memorization rather than genuine algorithmic execution.

Yes, there is a formal tension, and it does impose hard limits: a transformer with fixed depth d and precision p computes a function in the complexity class TC⁰ (threshold circuits of constant depth), which means it cannot faithfully implement any algorithm requiring more than O(1) sequential dependencies relative to input length — this is the result from Hahn (2020) and sharpened by Merrill & Sabharwal (2023, "The Parallelism Tradeoff"), who show that fixed-depth transformers cannot recognize even simple formal languages like DYCK-2 (balanced parentheses) with hard attention, precisely because checking arbitrary nesting depth requires sequential dependency chains longer than the circuit depth allows. The practical consequence is that multi-digit addition with n digits requires O(n) sequential carry propagation steps, which a depth-d transformer can only approximate up to n≈d — beyond that, it must either use scratchpad tokens to externalize the sequential state (effectively increasing circuit depth by adding computation steps) or memorize the answer via a shallow lookup that breaks at novel lengths. Deletang et al. (2023) make this concrete empirically by mapping tasks onto the Chomsky hierarchy: regular languages (finite automata, O(1) memory) generalize well, counter languages (requiring unbounded counting) fail systematically, and stack languages fail completely — the failure boundary tracks the sequential depth requirement almost perfectly across architectures and training procedures. The important nuance experts emphasize is that this is a representation limit, not just a learning limit — even with infinite data and perfect optimization, a 6-layer transformer cannot implement exact carry propagation for 100-digit addition in a single forward pass, because the required computational graph has sequential depth 100 and the architecture has depth 6, and no weight setting bridges that gap. Chain-of-thought / scratchpad sidesteps this by converting sequential depth into token length, making the transformer's parallel depth act repeatedly across generated tokens — each forward pass does O(1) sequential work, and O(n) passes handle O(n) depth — but this only works if each pass correctly conditions on previous outputs, which loops back to the faithfulness and bypass-circuit problems discussed earlier.

The weight of evidence strongly favors statistical shortcut over genuine algorithmic implementation: Dziri et al. (2023, "Faith and Fate: Limits of Transformers on Compositionality") show that GPT-4 on multi-step compositional reasoning tasks exhibits accuracy that degrades as a smooth function of compositional depth in a pattern consistent with approximate lookup rather than exact computation, and critically, performance collapses on structurally novel problem instances that share the same algorithm but differ in surface statistics from training data — exactly the signature of shortcut exploitation. The definitive evaluation design requires three components working together: first, distributional adversarial probing — construct test instances that are algorithmically identical to training examples but statistically out-of-distribution (e.g., using digit combinations that never co-occur in pretraining, or reversing the conventional left-to-right carry direction), which a true algorithm should handle identically but a shortcut should fail on. Second, systematic depth scaling — if the model is implementing the algorithm via a shallow circuit, accuracy should drop sharply at a specific problem size determined by circuit depth, whereas shortcut exploitation produces a smoother degradation curve whose slope encodes how quickly the test distribution diverges from training statistics; these curves have distinguishably different shapes. Third, and most decisively, mechanistic circuit analysis via activation patching — identify which attention heads are necessary and sufficient for correct answers by ablating heads layer by layer, then check whether the critical heads' attention patterns implement recognizable algorithmic primitives (carry lookup, digit alignment) or diffuse pattern-matching over surface features; Anthropic's interpretability work on toy models shows these two circuit types are visually and quantitatively distinguishable. The uncomfortable finding from applying these tests to large models is that you typically get neither pure answer — models appear to implement partial algorithmic structure (real carry-like circuits exist in early layers) combined with statistical smoothing that fills in gaps where the circuit is incomplete, making the binary question "algorithm or shortcut" ill-posed; the more precise question is what fraction of correct answers on the test set are generated by the algorithmic pathway versus the statistical pathway, and current evidence suggests this fraction decreases as problem size grows.
